TO:  Mayor and City Council
FROM:  Marcella Marlowe, Ph.D., City Manager
  Brian Haworth, Community Services Director
DATE:  April 30, 2021

SUBJECT: DISCUSSION AND DIRECTION REGARDING THE CITY’S 2021
  INDEPENDENCE DAY CELEBRATION PLANS

STRATEGIC PLAN CRITICAL SUCCESS FACTORS

• Engaged and Connected Residents
• Efficient, Responsive, and Effective City Services
• Fiscally Responsible and Transparent City Government

BACKGROUND

Historically, the City of San Marino hosts a grand Independence Day event annually on July 4th
of every given year. The day kicks off with the Blecksmith 5K Run, then continues with the
Independence Day Parade, and concludes with a program of events and fireworks at a full-to-
capacity Lacy Park fireworks show. (Please note that neither the run, nor the parade, is
sponsored by the City.) The event is the centerpiece of our community engagement efforts
throughout the year.

In 2020, the event was cancelled due to COVID-19. On March 5, 2021, I informed the City
Council that, sadly, we had again decided to cancel the 2021 event, due to a variety of
challenges presented by the timing to plan such an event and the County’s changing and
ambiguous protocols. Our decision mirrored that of most of our municipal neighbors, who had
also decided not to host a large scale community event yet.

Now, however, the County’s positioning has changed a bit and it does seem possible that the
City could hold something resembling our normal event, albeit significantly pared down.
Planning the event at this late date would cause significant impacts to staff and resources, so
City Council direction is requested.

  1-1
 DISCUSSION

There are a few general matters to take into consideration. First, this year, July 4th falls on a
Sunday. The legal holiday will be observed on Monday, July 5, 2021. This will create a long
weekend, meaning that many families may elect to travel that weekend and not be present in
San Marino for the potential celebration. Second, we’ve been informed that the Blecksmith 5K
will again be virtual this year. Finally, the Rotary Club reports that the parade will again be
cancelled this year.

Staff has spent much time understanding L.A. County’s health protocols for events such as this.
In fact, if it is the Council’s direction to proceed with this event, we are required to get the
County’s review and approval on our plans in advance.

Based on those guidelines, we have framed what the event could look like this year. Since this
is based on the County’s guidelines, please note that there is very little flexibility in any of these
parameters.

Programming. We would have a program beginning at 8pm, including a welcome from the
Mayor/City Council, introduction of San Marino National Little League (SMNLL) baseball all-
stars, and concert. The event would feature a full 20-minute fireworks show at 9pm. As of last
week, the community’s preferred vendor is available; we will confirm with him again on
Thursday afternoon, so that we have current information Friday morning for the City Council’s
consideration. Food trucks would be invited, but no City Club pavilion could be permitted.

Attendance. The estimated permitted capacity is 3,000 attendees. That number includes staff
needed to run the event and any programming participants (i.e. SMNLL all-stars, musicians,
vendors, etc.). It should be noted that that number might need to be reduced as a result of the
concert stage and/or the fireworks drop zone since capacity is based on how much space is
available.

Tickets. Tickets would be capped at 6 (see “Seating” section below) and would only be
conducted on a pre-registration basis; no “day of” tickets would be permitted. We would set a
registration deadline. If, at that point, interest exceeds the number of tickets available, we
would conduct a random lottery to determine who is able to acquire tickets. Please note: – in
2019, the total number of attendees was approximately 9,200, with approximately 6,300 of those
being San Marino residents.

Time of Event. The time frame for this event (counted from when attendees first arrive to
when they have all exited Lacy Park) would be limited to a maximum of four hours. Given the
need for at least semi-darkness when the fireworks start, we recommend the timeframe of
6pm-10pm; moving that earlier would not accommodate the fireworks show and time for
people to exit safely. Lacy Park would be closed all day; only those with tickets would be

  1-2
 admitted, and only beginning at 6pm for setting up. (This would mean that the tradition of
coming early with blankets would not be permitted, even for neighbors who have gates into
Lacy Park on their properties.) Food trucks would be available beginning at 7pm.

Seating. Squares that are 10’ x 10’ would be marked off with proper spacing within the park.
Each square would be able to accommodate a maximum of 6 people. Square locations would
be assigned in advance; attendees would not be able to select their own location – either in
advance or the day of the event (see above for more information). When not at the food
trucks, playground, or restroom area (where distancing is required), attendees would be
required to stay seated in their “square” and not mix with other families. Unfortunately, due to
the coordination requirements, it will not be feasible for us to have a “fully vaccinated” area.

Masking & Distancing. Face coverings are required, as is 6’ of distancing between parties.

Concluding Considerations. Planning an event of this scope, even with the pared-down
offerings, takes months. We typically begin planning for this event in late January/early
February. If we do offer this event, we would be three months behind. For staff to be able to
successfully host the event with the two months available, priorities in the Community Services
Department would need to be shuffled, with many work plan items postponed. This would
primarily impact reopening projects, pop-up events, and new programming (including virtual
programming), and would stretch staff very thin for even our daily operations.

There is also concern that this would not be the “community building” event that we are
accustomed to. Because of the required attendance limitations, we would need to turn away
half of the number of residents who typically attend. Intermingling would not be permitted.
And the other components of the celebration day – the Blecksmith Run and the Parade – will
not be occurring at all, or at least not in person. Although the program would look similar, the
event is not likely to “feel” like our normal program and not likely to bring our community
together the way we are accustomed to.

Finally, this would mark the first significant City function where adherence to the masking
protocols would be firmly required; if there are lapses in mask wearing, attendees will turn to
staff to enforce those protocols. I am concerned about our staff being put in the unwinnable
position of either enforcing the rules or not enforcing the rules – both would garner complaints
from the community. We have been able to avoid that dilemma so far, but this event, given the
scale, would be problematic.

For these reasons, Community Services Director Haworth and I recommend that this event be
cancelled.

  1-3
 FISCAL IMPACT & PROCUREMENT REVIEW

The projected cost for the event is approximately $77,000. Materials would cost an estimated
$35,000, with the majority of that coming from fireworks ($25,000). Staffing (community
services, police, fire, and public works) would cost an estimated $42,000.

We project a maximum estimated revenue of $15,000, given a $5.00 per person ticket charge
and a maximum of 3,000 attendees. This reflects our ongoing regular ticket price for residents
who purchase their tickets in advance. Given that this would be a significantly pared down
event, we certainly don’t feel comfortable charging more than we would in “regular” times.

Although no additional appropriation is necessary, this leaves a total net cost to the
City of approximately $62,000 if we host the event.

Procurement review is not applicable.

LEGAL REVIEW

The City Attorney has reviewed and approved this report as to form.

RECOMMENDATION

Staff recommends that the Fourth of July event be cancelled. If the City Council concurs with
staff’s recommendation, an appropriate motion would be:

“I move to cancel the 2021 Fourth of July event.”

In the event that the City Council directs that the event be held, staff requests confirmation or
direction regarding the following specific points:
  • Should ticket purchases be limited to San Marino residents only?
  • Should all attendees be limited to San Marino residents only?
  • Should the City charge $5 per ticket?

ATTACHMENTS

None.

SUBJECT:  PRESENTATION OF FY 2021-22  PROPOSED  OPERATING
  BUDGET BY DEPARTMENT

STRATEGIC PLAN CRITICAL SUCCESS FACTORS

• Engaged and Connected Residents
• Efficient, Responsive, and Effective City Services
• Fiscally Responsible and Transparent City Government

BACKGROUND

During the Fiscal Year 2019-20 budget process, staff worked together with the City Council
Budget Liaisons (then Council Members Jakubowski and Ude) to develop an innovative and
streamlined budget process that ultimately led to a successful adoption of the budget on May 31,
2019. The FY 2020-21 budget process followed a similar process, and the budget was successfully
adopted on June 26, 2020.

This year’s budget process is largely following the same process, but with one significant change.
Because of multiple difficulties that arose with the priority initiative process this year, staff had
discussions with the Budget Liaisons (Mayor Ude and Vice Mayor Jakubowski) and decided to
retire the priority initiative process and replace it with a more flexible goal-setting session and
community input survey. This has allowed staff to think about all suggestions from Council and
the community – whether it is a small process improvement or an expensive new program – and
truly assess which are feasible inclusions in each department’s complete workplan for the year.

To date, the following actions have taken place to put us on the right footing for today’s
presentation of the FY 2021-22 proposed budget by department operational expenditures:

  •  At the January 29, 2021 City Council meeting, City Council was given a mid-year status
  update on the five Fiscal Year 2020-21 priority initiatives, and then conducted a free-form
  goal-setting session to discuss their goals and visions for the upcoming fiscal year.

  2-1
   •  In February, staff took the goals brainstormed by City Council and created a community
  survey and hosted a virtual town hall. In past years, the community only voted on which
  Council or staff-driven ideas they were most interested in. This year, staff created a survey
  that allowed community members write in their own ideas based on each of our eight
  Critical Success Factors and express their level of interest for each Council idea. The
  survey was translated into Chinese and was open for the entire month of February. At
  the end of the month, staff had 43 responses. Staff went through each of these ideas and
  assessed the feasibility of incorporating them into their workplans. A summary of
  Council’s ideas, the community’s interest level in those, new ideas proposed by the
  community, and staff’s response regarding if they were incorporated into their FY 2021-
  22 workplan is attached here as Attachment 1.

  •  On February 26, 2021, staff presented the mid-year review, five-year financial forecast,
  and long-term financial projection.

  •  On March 19 and 26, 2021 City Council reviewed and gave direction on the FY 2021-22
  Capital Equipment and Improvement Budget.

DISCUSSION

Today’s meeting continues the next stage of the budget process. Over the course of two meetings
(April 30 and May 7), the City Council will review the expenditure side of the FY 2021-22
proposed operating budget and work plans, as well as following up on pending items from the
Capital Improvement Plan. Staff will provide a high-level budget summary, anticipated fund balance
and revenue details during the presentation in order to help frame the discussion.

The attachments to this staff report include each department’s budget packet, including budget
memorandum, narrative description, current year accomplishments, next year’s objectives, up-
to-date operating dashboard, and the operating budget documents broken out into Personnel
and Services & Supplies sections.

FY 2021-22 Proposed Revenue Budget

The proposed revenue budget for FY 2021-22 is $33,736,980, which represents a $1.4M or 4%
increase from the current budget. The largest revenue increase is reflected in the General Fund,
which includes the $1.2M American Rescue Plan Act of 2021.

As the Council is aware, personnel costs make up approximately 68% of the operating budget
($19.6M). There are no increases proposed to staffing levels in this budget; this means that all
changes in personnel costs for FY 2021-22 result from previously negotiated contractual
increases or non-discretionary items like CalPERS pension expenses. The Personnel budget does
include the approved salary schedule for part-time employees and the 1.0 FTE Code Enforcement
Officer position in Community Development (approved by City Council during the February 10,
2021 City Council Meeting) and a 2% increase for part-time employees as directed by Council.

The remaining 30% of the operating budget ($8.5M) is devoted to Services & Supplies, with a
proposed increase of approximately $532K or 7%. The proposed budget includes the following
Council/Community goals for FY 2021-22:

  •  The inclusion of $40,000 for a citywide marketing and branding campaign.

  •  An increase of $600,000 for preparation of the General Plan Update.

While there are some discretionary changes that the City Council may review, it should be noted
that many of these expenses are contractually obligated, with built-in CPI increases. The main
discretionary expenditures for the City Council to address occur in the Capital budget. While
many of those decisions were made by the Council on March 17 (CIP – Equipment) and March
26 (CIP – Infrastructure), and pending items from the Capital Improvement Plan will be discussed
during the May 7 City Council meeting.

Staff will be available to answer specific questions at the meeting.

RECOMMENDATION

Staff recommends that the City Council provide direction to the City Manager on the proposed
FY 2021-22 operating budget.

DEPARTMENT PURPOSE

The mission of the Mayor and City Council is to provide leadership to the community through the
establishment of policies which enhance the quality of life for San Marino residents, businesses, non-profit
institutions, and other stakeholders; and to maintain a strong and stable fiscal condition.

DEPARTMENT DESCRIPTION

The City Council consists of five members, typically elected at large to four-year terms. The Mayor and
Vice Mayor are council members selected by the Council, traditionally for a one-year term. The City
Council is responsible for setting policies, passing ordinances and resolutions, adopting the budget,
appointing committee members, hiring the City Manager and City Attorney, and concurring in the
appointment of department heads.

Because the Mayor and City Council are the legislative representatives of the City, all citywide
memberships are assigned to their budget. These memberships include the League of California Cities,
League of California Cities, Los Angeles County Division, the San Gabriel Valley Council of Government,
and the Southern California Association of Governments. These memberships make up almost 70% of the
City Council budget each fiscal year. The remaining City Council expenditures are for travel and meetings,
City Council hosted events, and materials and supplies such as name plates, business cards, and plaques.

  PARKS AND PUBLIC WORKS DEPARTMENT

DEPARTMENT PURPOSE

The mission of the City of San Marino Parks and Public Works Department is to create and sustain our
precious community assets.

DEPARTMENT DESCRIPTION

The Parks and Public Works Department is responsible for the design, construction, maintenance and
operations of the city’s public infrastructure, and performs this mission through a combination of physical
assets, best management practices and policies, and skilled personnel. The City’s infrastructure assets
include:

  •  121 lane-miles of public street and alley rights-of-way (curbs, gutters, sidewalks, signs, traffic signals
  and street lighting)
  •  60 acres of landscaping including Lacy Park and boulevard-style median parks (Huntington Drive,
  Sierra Madre Boulevard and Old Mill Road)
  •  65,000 square feet of civic facilities including city hall, police station, fire station, Public Works
  corporation yard, San Marino Center, Stoneman, Crowell Public Library, 7 municipal parking lots,
  and historic buildings such as the Old Mill and the Thurnher House
  •  51 miles of wastewater collection system including sewer mains, manholes and 3 lift stations
  •  6 miles of stormwater drainage system including lined and unlined washes, culverts, manholes and
  drainage inlets

The Department is composed of seven divisions: Administration (including city engineering), Right-of-Way
(also called Streets), Fleet, Sewer (wastewater and stormwater), Parks, Grounds, and Building
Maintenance.

FISCAL YEAR 2020-21 ACCOMPLISHMENTS

  •  Completed the replacement of the 1980s Lacy Park restroom on budget

  •  Completed the citywide traffic circulation study including the neighborhood traffic calming

  •  Completed the assessment of the City’s stormwater system
  •  Fumigated the City Hall campus (City Hall and Police and Fire Stations) and renovated the interior

  •  Commenced the design to renovate San Marino Center including preparation of a focused

DEPARTMENT PURPOSE

The mission of the San Marino Fire Department is to save lives and property, and ensure the safety of our
community.

DEPARTMENT DESCRIPTION

The Fire Department’s primary purpose is to provide lifesaving emergency response for fire suppression
and emergency medical services for residents of the City. Equally important, however, are its
responsibilities in the areas of fire prevention, life safety inspections, community education and emergency
preparedness.

The delivery of life saving paramedic services is an integral part of the Fire Department mission. All of the
San Marino firefighters are licensed Paramedics trained to the highest level provided within the County of
Los Angeles. Only about ten percent of the cities in Los Angeles County employ paramedics with the
extensive training and experience required to provide advanced life support using standing field treatment
protocols.

Other services include:

  •  Annual inspections of commercial property and school occupancy
  •  Review of commercial and large residential building plans for adequacy of fire detection and
  suppression systems
  •  Pre-incident exercises and training with allied agencies, and others related to high-risk or high-
  value areas of the City, such as the High Fire Hazard Severity Zone and the Huntington Library,
  Art Collections and Botanical Gardens
  •  Participation in public education in schools, neighborhoods, community groups and service clubs
  to stress fire safety, first aid, cardiopulmonary resuscitation and emergency preparedness
  •  In conjunction with the South Pasadena Fire Department, share fire command Chief Officers for
  the two fire departments. By sharing resources, the fire departments can provide an enhanced
  service at a lower cost
  •  In conjunction with MySafe California, a non-profit safety organization, the San Marino Fire
  Department conducts a Junior Fire Program for Huntington Middle School, and cardio pulmonary
  resuscitation (CPR) training for San Marino High School students
  •  Emergency Management responsibilities for the City

FISCAL YEAR 2020-21 ACCOMPLISHMENTS

  •  Coordinated the City of San Marino’s response to COVID-19, including the activation of the City’s
  Emergency Operations Center; proclamation of a local disaster by the San Marino City Council
  on March 17, 2020; approval by the City Council of the City’s Disease Pandemic Response Plan;
  coordination of the City’s Crisis Communications Committee; and leading the City’s Recovery
  Leadership Team
  •  Researched, prepared, and ordered a new rescue ambulance as part of the City’s approved Fiscal
  Year 2020-21 Capital Improvement Plan. Due to COVID restrictions with the manufacturer,
  delivery of the rescue ambulance is anticipated in FY 2021-22.
